correctness.rationale: For KG(n,2), vertices are 2-subsets of [n] and adjacency is disjointness. The initial observed set consists of the selected vertices and all 2-sets disjoint from a selected edge; a white 2-set must meet every selected edge. No single vertex dominates by the update rule. At n=5 precisely 30 intersecting pairs initially force the remaining vertices. For n>=6 no pair suffices. With >=3 selected edges, either their common endpoint is absent, so the remaining white 2-sets form a (possibly empty) set of at most two that can be forced from observed vertices, or all selected edges form a star. A star with k spokes leaves precisely the white incident 2-sets and forces iff n-1-k<=3 (equivalently k>=n-4). Thus for n>=8 the only unsuccessful k>=3 sets are k-edge stars with 3<=k<=n-5; they are uniquely centered and counted by n*C(n-1,k). Every nonstar triple is minimal, and n-4-spoke stars are the additional minimal sets when n>=8. Total minimal-set count C(C(n,2),3) for n>=6 follows from cancellation. Independent direct-definition forcing and coefficient counts were executed for ALL 2^10 n=5 subsets, ALL 2^15 n=6 subsets and all k<=3 subsets at n=7,8,9: 46,844 sets, no mismatches. These finite tests corroborate, but the structural white-pair proof establishes the all-n result.

value.rationale: Power domination measures propagation-assisted observability rather than static coverage, so exact coefficients and inclusion-minimal sensors in the highly symmetric Kneser KG(n,2) family are motivated. The failure criterion and n-4-spoke threshold yield a nontrivial family-size transition while the total number of minimal solutions remains invariant; neither minimum cardinality nor a generic polynomial definition gives this distribution. This is an exact structural classification for infinitely many graphs, not a gratuitous special-case computation.
